claims.text: The initial FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is synthesized by arc-melting under an inert atmosphere with minimal interstitial oxygen.
Introducing a controlled amount of oxygen during FeNiCrMn processing will promote ordered oxygen complexes.
Ordered oxygen complexes impede dislocation motion.
Controlled oxygen doping will enhance both yield strength and ductility relative to inert-processed FeNiCrMn.
A slight oxygen partial pressure during arc-melting can be used to achieve controlled oxygen doping.
Multiple arc-melting/remelting steps followed by room-temperature tensile testing constitute an applicable processing and testing workflow.
Elevated-temperature mechanical testing can be used to evaluate the proposed oxygen-induced mechanical benefits.
XRD and TEM can detect the proposed ordered oxygen complexes in FeNiCrMn.
Interstitial oxygen atoms segregate into ordered complexes within the alloy matrix.
The oxygen complexes provide solid-solution strengthening by acting as barriers to dislocation motion.
Interstitial oxygen contributes to energy dissipation through Snoek-type relaxation.
Dislocation blocking and Snoek-type relaxation collectively improve strength and ductility.
Oxygen-doped FeNiCrMn will show statistically significant increases in yield strength and ductility relative to the inert control.
The beneficial mechanical effects will occur only within a narrow range of oxygen content.
An inert-processed FeNiCrMn baseline with negligible oxygen will lack ordered interstitial complexes.
Excess oxygen can produce undesirable oxide phases and embrittlement.
The magnitude of mechanical improvement depends on oxygen content and processing parameters.
Absence of statistically significant strength and ductility improvements, or absence of ordered oxygen complexes, would falsify the hypothesis.
